items.title: Cupertino kicks off with an audacious and entertaining series premiere
items.author: Saloni Gajjar

items.text:
To say that the AI boom has caused a certain level of existential dread is not an understatement, mainly because it’s being spearheaded and controlled by a chosen few without much regulation (for now). It’s become a hot button topic, and Cupertino thankfully isn’t subtle about which side it’s on. In the opening seconds of Robert and Michelle King‘s’ legal dramedy, attorney Michael Price (Mike Colter) packs up his desk after he’s fired from a tech startup that he invested in. The first item in his filing box? A chocolate bar named David. At episode’s end, Michael states that the mission of his brand new law firm—which he launches alongside lawyer Olivia Siffre (Rachel Keller)—is akin to the David vs. Goliath saga. That is, they’re the heroic underdogs facing off against powerful Silicon Valley companies. They’ll only take on clients no one else will out of fear of pissing off the Goliaths. With that, Cupertino sets up its resonant premise: It will examine tech’s unavoidable encroachment into our lives, and its extremely harmful influence.


It all starts with, as the episode’s title suggests, “Michael And Olivia.” The two are let go from the successful S-Talk on the same day for different, shady reasons. Michael is falsely accused of proprietary leaks so his co-founder, Richard Everett (Will Brill), can keep Michael’s equity; Olivia is fired before she can tell anyone Richard sexually harassed her by sending her a dick pic. Wrongfully terminated by and angry at their employer, Michael and Olivia team up to bring two lawsuits against S-Talk. However, Olivia is resistant at first, knowing that her traditional family wouldn’t want her to make public such a private matter. It’s not until she finds out that Richard modeled Daisy—his next-level generative AI model—after her that Olivia decides to fight back.


Cupertino gives Olivia a lot of layers right away: She’s a religious conservative who prays often and keeps a Bible at her desk; she’s also open-minded and couldn’t wait to leave her Wisconsin hometown after graduation; she’s soft-spoken and therefore frequently underestimated. The Kings infuse her with a lot of personality, including her love of musicals. (She hums Annie‘s “It’s A Hard Knock Life” whenever she’s nervous, which is the kind of character detail that quickly helps the audience understand her.) Best known for her work in grittier dramas like Legion, Tokyo Vice, and The Society, Keller brings an admirable tenderness to the character. Colter matches her performance, mixing Michael’s swagger with vulnerability. The Evil actor straddles Michael’s professional ambitions, family pressures, and morality.


Unlike his wealthy celebrity lawyer father, Bayard (Joe Morton)—who drops in just to chastise his son—Michael doesn’t want to represent bigwigs. Instead, he hopes to stand for those wronged by Big Tech heavyweights. So he encourages Olivia to do the same without being pushy or demanding. Michael and Olivia end up getting along swimmingly, working out their respective lawsuits from an IHOP until Michael’s spunky, resourceful assistant helps them out. Christy Palladino (Ella Stiller)—also fired from S-Talk—joins the two lawyers, using her blue-collar family’s contacts to secure them a lavish workspace. Or rather, a fancy reception area, because the actual cubicles inside the building don’t exist yet. Once the firm starts making money, the plan is to build one room after another. Until then, the chic lobby will have to do.


Once “Michael And Olivia” heads to court, Richard’s lawyer (played by Steven Pasquale) gives them a hard time. Still, Michael and Olivia put up a solid fight. Most of the argument boils down to Richard’s mortifying new gen-AI creation, Daisy, whose voice and “personality” are freakishly similar to that of Olivia, who clarifies that she trained Daisy as part of an assignment; she didn’t know Richard was essentially cloning her. All of this derails S-Talk’s 14-day deadline to raise funds, especially since Olivia also points out that the company’s biggest VC donor has spoken out against DEI (so it looks worse that their only Black lawyer was fired).


At the end of all this, Richard and Ry end up offering a whole lot of money in a settlement deal. We don’t see the exact number, but it’s enough for Michael, Olivia, and Christy to celebrate that they can now officially kick off this law firm and start seeking clients. Just as Michael and Olivia jot down and sign their 50-50 partnership on a pillar, the elevator dings and in walks a bewildered new client (played by Nik Dodani) desperately seeking their help.


As far as series premieres go, Cupertino is both exciting and essential. Directed by Robert King and co-written by the husband-wife duo, it succeeds at not only introducing and fleshing out the world and those who populate it, but most importantly, puts forth the show’s vision in a crystal clear way. Michael and Olivia might have lost the battle (the judge did side with Richard in Olivia’s lawsuit, and Michael’s was settled out of court), but Cupertino is sure shaping them to win the war.


Stray observations:

• Debra Monk and David Aaron Baker guest star as Olivia’s parents, who rush to California to bring their daughter home after she’s fired and appear skeptical of her partnership with Michael.


• There’s a funny running gag throughout this episode wherein the strangers Michael meets (his cab driver, the process server, etc.) pitch him ideas for their shopping, catering, and ride share startups.


• The fledgling firm hires actors to fool Richard and Ry into thinking it’s already successful and potentially backed by Bayard. Good thinking!


• Once Michael finds out Olivia has a thing for musicals, he sends her a playlist so she can listen to “real music,” and it’s composed of songs by Fantastic Negrito.


• Try not to feel total and complete terror at the following defense that Ry gives for S-Talk in court about their AI principles in an effort to prove that Daisy isn’t based on Olivia: “We train from everyone’s personalities online. Millions of people from Reddit, X, Meta, from novels, articles, and on Zoom. It’s the grand melting pot of AI. It’s called fair use.”

Saloni Gajjar is The A.V. Club‘s TV critic.

items.title: “Cupertino” is a Smart Big Tech Procedural
items.author: Jen Chaney
items.summary: Movie theaters are currently inundated with major motion pictures that examine and/or indict the behavior of wealthy Silicon Valley leaders, including Meta’s
items.text:
Movie theaters are currently inundated with major motion pictures that examine and/or indict the behavior of wealthy Silicon Valley leaders, including Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg (“The Social Reckoning”), Theranos fraudster Elizabeth Holmes (“You Can See Everything”), Elon Musk (Alex Gibney’s “Musk”), and OpenAI’s Sam Altman (“Artificial”). Television is in on the trend, too. In November, Netflix will remind us of the implosion of cryptocurrency fund FTX and its founder, Sam Bankman-Fried, in “The Altruists.”

On CBS and Paramount+ starting Thursday, there’s “Cupertino,” a broadcast-network procedural that doesn’t zero in on a real-life tech bro, but does raise a lot of sobering questions about the industry currently attempting to cram A.I. down the throats of the global populace.

Created by Michelle and Robert King—the showrunning power couple responsible for “The Good Wife,” “The Good Fight,” “Evil,” “Elsbeth,” and ensuring that CBS still offers quality programming in primetime—the series is a legal drama about an upstart law firm that focuses specifically on clients who want to sue powerful Silicon Valley companies.

“I’m sick of people controlling my fate, and my guess is there are a lot of people out there that feel the same way but don’t have anyone to represent them,” says Michael Price (Mike Colter of “Luke Cage” and “Evil”), an attorney who co-founded, then got edged out of, an extremely successful big tech company called S-Talk.

He’s explaining his reasons for wanting to start an agency that takes on the cases against Magnificent 7-level companies that other firms are too afraid to touch. But he could just as easily be describing this show’s appeal to an American audience frustrated by the unemployment rate, the disproportionate power and wealth of the billionaire class, and the non-stop insistence that everyone get on board with artificial intelligence.

Unlike the other projects mentioned above, “Cupertino” does not focus on the idiosyncrasies/neuroses of a single, perceived “genius.” It is more general in its depiction of big tech, which enables it to feel both timely and, perhaps, more relatable to the average person.

Pictured (L-R): Rachel Keller as Olivia Siffre and Mike Colter as Michael Price. Photo: Elizabeth Fisher/CBS ©2026 CBS Broadcasting, Inc. All Rights Reserved.

While there are some key storylines that run throughout the first 10 episodes—the rivalry between Michael and his showboating lawyer father (Joe Morton); another, separate rivalry between Michael and his ex, also an attorney (Renée Elise Goldsberry, who co-starred opposite Colter on “Evil”); and, most importantly, an ongoing narrative about a particularly dangerous form of AI—this is largely a case-of-the-week type of show.

With its quick, plot-driven pacing, “Cupertino” is episodic, mainstream network storytelling that shows, like so much of the Kings’ output, that it’s still possible to make smart, sophisticated, digestible television within that framework.

As Michael, Colter is dignified, pragmatic and, if I’m being honest, not wildly different in demeanor from David, the priest the actor played on “Evil.” But he’s a persuasive lead in both shows, so I’m not going to complain too much about any overlap. While Michael believes in justice and the rule of law, he’s not some anti-capitalist hero who wants to burn down all of Silicon Valley. He simply sees a gap in the marketplace that needs filling. “When you’re in the middle of the ocean, you don’t sell people more water,” he explains to Goldsberry’s Nichole. “You sell them life jackets.”

His partner at the new firm, Olivia Siffre (Rachel Keller), a devout Christian and gifted lawyer who also gets fired from S-Talk after being sexually harassed by the head of the company, is the bleeding heart in this pairing. Keller and Colter have an organic, friendly chemistry that, to the show’s credit, is supportive without being romantic, at least not in these early episodes.

But the standout performances in “Cupertino” come from the two actors who provide the most comedic relief in a drama that doesn’t shy away from poking fun at the always-pitching culture of venture capitalism. Ella Stiller (daughter of Ben Stiller and Christine Taylor) gets a break-out role as Christy Palladino, a third employee who gets fired from S-Talk and becomes the receptionist at Price and Siffre, where she proves to be a fantastic investigator for her attorney bosses.

Christy is particularly adept at tracking down leads and calling in favors from her extensive family of blue-collar workers; after being escorted out of the S-Talk building, she phones her electrician uncle, who proceeds to turn the power on and off in that office and enrage everyone still “lucky” enough to be employed there. Christy knows nothing about technology, but she loves to stick it to the man. Her default expression is resting “you’ve got to be kidding me” face, and Stiller has got that expression down pat.

Pictured (L-R): Ella Stiller as Christy Palladino, Mike Colter as Michael Price, and Rachel Keller as Olivia Siffre. Photo: Elizabeth Fisher/CBS ©2026 CBS Broadcasting, Inc. All Rights Reserved

Then there’s Busy Phillips, who’s cast as Natalia Boutella, a key investor in the new firm who also happens to be divorced from a tech executive played by Fisher Stevens who is not Jeff Bezos, but also is totally Jeff Bezos. Natalia is less interested in sticking it to the man than she is in sticking it to that particular man. When he denies that he has gained weight after she tells him he “got fat,” Natalia counters: “You dined with the president, you had a front row seat to that inauguration, you bought a billion-dollar yacht. You got fat.” Phillips utters lines like that as if they’re coated in venom.

(As an added bonus, every time she and Goldsberry appear in the same scene, it’s like a partial “Girls5Eva” reunion, and that alone deserves a fresh designation on Rotten Tomatoes.)

The Kings and co. tackle numerous zeitgeisty tech trends; one episode focuses on a teenager compelled to kill his father by a chatbot, while another, which happens to debut less than a week before the midterms, zeroes in on prediction websites used to manipulate elections.

But “Cupertino” is not a purely anti-A.I. narrative. The episodes also highlight situations where technological assistance can help. Television is in on the trend, too. In November, Netflix will remind us of the implosion of cryptocurrency fund FTX and its founder, Sam Bankman-Fried, in “The Altruists.”

Created by Michelle and Robert King—the showrunning power couple responsible for “The Good Wife,” “The Good Fight,” “Evil,” “Elsbeth,” and ensuring that CBS still offers quality programming in primetime—the series is a legal drama about an upstart law firm that focuses specifically on clients who want to sue powerful Silicon Valley companies.

He’s explaining his reasons for wanting to start an agency that takes on the cases against Magnificent 7-level companies that other firms are too afraid to touch. But he could just as easily be describing this show’s appeal to an American audience frustrated by the unemployment rate, the disproportionate power and wealth of the billionaire class, and the non-stop insistence that everyone get on board with artificial intelligence.

items.author: Angharad Redden

items.text:
Published Oct 9, 2026, 6:02 AM EDT

Known as 'Cyberpunk 2077's' biggest fan, Angharad is a Welsh games writer who thrives in anything related to digital storytelling. If a video game explores the intricacies and horrors of womanhood, she is there.
Thanks to previous work at GAMINGbible, GameByte, The Loadout, Game Luster, Angharad has built a strong understanding of both the digital world and what fans want from it and is eager to share her thoughts and expertise with readers.

In recent months, Xbox has been in our good books, at least compared to its PlayStation competitor. Set to welcome Hideo Kojima's highly anticipated IP, Physint, as well as reports that it is currently working on the next Xbox generation titled Project Helix, it is an exciting time to be an Xbox fan.

However, the good news does not end there, as from now until 11 October, Xbox is giving its users the chance to grab seven games for absolutely free. The catch is that some of them will require an Xbox Game Pass subscription, whilst others are a timed trial only. However, this gives you the perfect excuse to try before you buy, especially as they all come alongside a steep discount as part of the Free Play Days event. So, if you are looking for something new to play and do not want to spend a single penny, look no further than the Xbox Store.

7
Screamer

In this high-octane racing game with anime graphics, players can expect "fighting mechanics and a story that hits hard." First released back in March, Screamer introduces a twist to the racing genre as players take to a world where some race for glory, and others race to seek power or even revenge. As such, every race is a fight for survival and every battle is personal. Receiving positive reviews at launch, this thrilling racing game is definitely an underrated gem of 2026.

6
Family Man

In this 2020 adventure RPG, expect a whole lot of crime and violence as you push the limits of your morality and take on questionable deeds in order to protect your family. Family Man is a dark, story-led RPG first released back in 2020 that will see you owe money to the mob, and you have just three weeks to earn it or your body may be found in the nearest river. No pressure. Take on dirty jobs, help the locals, and most importantly, do not get caught in a world where your choices can affect the very outcome of the story.

5
ARC Raiders

One of 2025's most talked about titles is now available to try for free as players experience PvP and PvE combat in this hit extraction shooter. ARC Raiders is still alive and well as players team up, or go it alone, to fight for resources and most importantly, get out alive in order to secure the best loot, make upgrades, and then do it all over again. With positive reviews upon launch, and multiple updates added over the past year, there has never been a better time to get stuck into this hit extraction shooter as it celebrates its first anniversary.

4
High on Life 2

Released back in February, High on Life 2 takes place in a world where an intergalactic conspiracy threatens everybody's fate, but luckily, you will get to team up with a group of alien guns to stab, shoot and skate your way through exotic and colorful environments to take down the bad guys and save humanity itself. With stunning environments, a lot of chaos and hours of fun to be had, High on Life 2 is a game you must experience for yourself.

3
Stalker 2: Heart of Chornobyl

As the fourth main title in the S.T.A.L.K.E.R. series, Stalker 2: Heart of Chornobyl released back in 2024 and saw players enter the Chornobyl Anomalous Zone in order to fight anomalies, mutants, and fellow survivors. In this post-apocalyptic FPS, you will need to explore, scavenge and, most importantly, survive in a bleak landscape and an environment that tries to fight back at every opportunity. With a recent overhaul thanks to Version 2.0, now is the perfect time to get stuck in, and Stalker 2: Heart of Chornobyl is available on Xbox as part of a timed trial.

2
Little Nightmares III

As the third installment in the cute, yet horrifying, atmospheric adventure game, you will take on the role of Low and Alone, two best friends who must work together to escape the Nowhere. Released back in October 2025, Little Nightmares III can be played solo with an AI companion, or with a friend, as you work together to solve puzzles and escape nightmarish creatures who will do anything to stop your escape. It may not be considered the best entry in the franchise, but being free as part of a timed trial will give you the perfect opportunity to make your own mind up.

1
Rogue Waters

Last, but by no means least, is Rogue Waters. In this 2024 turn-based tactics experience, players will live out their pirate fantasies as they take on the role of Captain Cutter and command a ship and its crew through procedurally generated encounters. As you upgrade your crew, you will need to train and recruit in order to create the best crew around, even going as far as to recruit powerful sea creatures to your side. Featuring dynamic naval combat and melee combat, Rogue Waters seems to be everything that Skull and Bones could not.

items.text:
Steam 9/10 Horror Hit Is Free To Keep Forever Until October 12

Published Oct 9, 2026, 5:48 AM EDT

Paul Farrelly is a Contributing Writer for Screen Rant’s Gaming section and the founder of GeekGasm.org, a site dedicated to celebrating all things gaming, from triple A blockbusters to weird and wonderful indie hits. Based in Louth, Ireland, Paul has spent years writing about games, pop culture, and tech, turning his lifelong love of gaming into a career that lets him talk (probably too much) about what makes this industry so endlessly fascinating.
He’s previously written and collaborated with several entertainment outlets, including LADbible, gaining a wide perspective on how gaming fits into today’s pop culture conversation. His work blends genuine enthusiasm with thoughtful analysis, exploring how design, storytelling, and community have made gaming one of the most creative mediums around.
When he’s not glued to a controller or keyboard, Paul’s usually spinning vinyl, plotting his next horror marathon, or debating which Resident Evil entry really reigns supreme.

We are now well into October 2026, so it's officially spooky season for most. And while many spend their evenings hanging Halloween decorations or carving pumpkins, some of us gamers like to spend our evenings playing horror titles. There's nothing quite like spending a fall evening unlocking new fears you never knew you had and self inflicting some psychological trauma in the process. The horror genre in gaming is quite crowded, but Steam is offering a game you can try for free and keep forever. So all you have to lose is your time and perhaps your mind!

Made by a small Indie developer, better known for the award-winning Inscryption, this horror title is where it all started for Daniel Mullins Games. What starts as a cheerful side scroller soon descends into chaos with you battling the devil himself in Pony Island. Similar to games like Inscryption, Doki-Doki Literature Club and Buckshot Roulette, Pony Island appears to be one type of game on the surface but soon becomes something much darker and malevolent. An arcade platformer that turns into a battle with the devil himself. Sign me up!

Pony Island first hit our screens over 10 years ago. Not relying on jump scares, the game is a slow-burn psychological horror game. If you've ever played its successor Inscryption, you'll know exactly the kind of dark undertones to expect. In fact, Pony Island at its heart is a horror puzzle game. The arcade game has been rigged by the devil, so you must solve puzzles and fix the underlying broken gaming code in order to succeed and ultimately save your soul.

Pony Island goes deeper than most horror titles though. Posing as a cursed game, it will break the fourth wall and leave you wondering if, in fact, your own computer has been infected. Without giving away any spoilers, there are moments during the gameplay where you'll feel very unsettled throughout the roughly 4-hour experience. As the game so aptly puts it, you need to break the machine, before it breaks you!

Steam

Getting Pony Island for free on Steam feels like the perfect treat for Halloween. While most horror titles rely on cheap jump scares or gory on-screen violence, Pony Island strips all that away and makes the player feel unsettled and unsafe. It truly gets under your skin and now that it's free on Steam, hopefully a new generation of players will get to experience it for the first time. It's also a timely release, with a sequel set to launch in April 2027. Pony Island 2: Panda Circus looks set to unnerve us all over again next year.

There are quite a number of great games for free on Steam, but there are also a lot of not so great ones. Pony Island firmly sits in the former category and now that it's free to play, there is no excuse for any lovers of creepy horror games to hit the download button. Games like Grand Theft Auto VI and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake can wait. I've got a side-scrolling pony and a battle with the devil to keep me busy this month! Pony Island is free to download on Steam today.

January 4, 2016

items.text:
Godzilla Minus Zero Review: The Sequel Loses Sight Of What Made 2023's Kaiju Epic Work

The sequel to one of the greatest Godzilla stories ever told is decidedly less impactful than the original, with a convoluted narrative.

Published Oct 9, 2026, 5:18 AM EDT

Ben is a Senior Writer on the New TV team at Screen Rant. He graduated from the University of Central Lancashire with a First Class B.A. Degree in English Literature and History.
Born and raised in Ireland, Ben has always had a love for storytelling in all forms of media and operates multiple projects under the name Benjamin Blogs. Ben is a comic book writer and podcast host, in addition to his work as an entertainment journalist. He has worked as both a writer and editor for Screen Rant, Collider, and other media outlets across various departments, including features, news, reviews, and interviews.

As a fan of Takashi Yamazaki's Godzilla Minus One, I was more than ready to get behind Godzilla Minus Zero, but unfortunately, this film didn't improve the legacy. Kaiju stories have been a staple on the big screen since long before I was born, with the original Japanese films inspiring numerous remakes and iterations both before and after the 1998 film, titled simply Godzilla, that was my earliest experience with the concept.

Since then, I have had the pleasure of diving deeper into the space, and many of these movies lean more into the genre of action and fantasy than something with drama or a well-defined story. However, Godzilla Minus One easily became one of my favorites in the genre, thanks to an intensely rich and moving narrative structure. It appears that movie will remain the peak.

Godzilla Minus Zero Proves Takashi Yamazaki Is A Gifted Filmmaker

A huge amount of credit and recognition should go to the extraordinary work that writer, director, and visual effects supervisor Takashi Yamazaki has put into this sequel. items.title: Damn, This GTA 6 Screenshot Looks So Good People Don’t Believe It’s Real
items.author: Zack Zwiezen

items.text:
Earlier today, Rockstar Games shared new information about the music and radio stations that will appear in Grand Theft Auto 6. Included with that news were a few new screenshots. And one particular screenshot featuring cars on a rainy street at night has got people freaking out and wondering if GTA 6 will actually look like this on consoles. And the answer is, yeah, probably. Mostly.

On October 8, Rockstar revealed that numerous famous musicians, including Bad Bunny, would host some of the radio stations in GTA 6. We also got our first official confirmation of some of these stations and what kinds of music they’ll play, and learned that you’ll be able to listen to all of them on foot via your phone. But on the website sharing all this info, a background screenshot of GTA 6 caught many people’s attention, including my own. Here’s a direct link to a super high-res version of it.

In the screenshot, we can spot a few different cars and people on a rainy street somewhere in the heart of Vice City at night. In the background, the neon lights of the Ocean View Hotel light up the buildings and wet pavement. And in the puddles, you can spot reflections of cars and other parts of the environment. It’s truly impressive, and fans online are freaking out over how good it looks while others are worried it might not be real or is doctored to look better than anything the actual game can produce when running on a PS5 in November.

“Ain’t no way that first screenshot is real; it looks so good,” replied one person on social media.

“Thought these were renders, but actual shots?” asked another user.

Digital Foundry’s Oliver Mackenzie weighed in on the matter when pinged by GTA content creator Ben VideoTech, and suggested that Rockstar may be using some sort of debug photo mode that would allow them to turn up resolution and settings to make the shot look as good as possible. However, as pointed out by Mackenzie, if you look at the screenshot closely, you can start to notice some visual faults that suggest it could be a shot captured from the game running on PS5 Pro. But “it’s not really possible to tell.”

For example, reflections further back in the image show obvious dithering, something we see all the time on reflections in most console games in 2026. You can also spot that shadows aren’t being drawn under pedestrians in the far distance. And if you look really far in the background and zoom in a lot, you can even spot what look like lower-poly people standing around.

In the past, Rockstar has generally used real, in-game and in-engine footage and screenshots of its upcoming games for marketing screenshots and trailers. I remember when GTA V was coming out, people looked at screenshots of the game and swore Rockstar was using touched-up images or running the game on high settings on PC. However, looking back at GTA V‘s Xbox 360 screenshots in 2026, it’s very clear these were taken in the game. Perhaps captured using a debug tool that let Rockstar turn up some settings and add some extra lights and poses, but GTA V‘s pre-release shots are very representative of what the game looked like on Xbox 360 and PS3. This is true of other Rockstar titles, too, like Red Dead, Bully, and Max Payne 3.

I think what’s likely happened here is that Rockstar is running the game on a PS5 Pro devkit and is using some sort of debug menu to take a super-crisp screenshot of the game at its highest possible resolution. So while the final game might rarely look this perfect and clean, I do think that, yeah, GTA 6 is going to look incredible at night on PS5, PS5 Pro, and Xbox Series X. As for Xbox Series S, well, good luck, my friends.

items.author: Simon Abrams
items.summary: The feature-length toy commercial Matchbox: The Movie, co-produced by Mattel Studios and Skydance executives like David Ellison, suggests that all the wrong
items.text:
The feature-length toy commercial Matchbox: The Movie, co-produced by Mattel Studios and Skydance executives like David Ellison, suggests that all the wrong lessons were learned from Greta Gerwig’s self-aware comedy fantasy Barbie. This ostensibly humorous stunt showcase flounders hardest whenever its quippy but capable protagonists use self-conscious humor and soulless melodramatic shorthand to pay tribute to the Matchbox line of toy cars and vehicles.


Director Sam Hargrave (Extraction and its sequel) and his capable stunt team predictably nail a few of the movie’s fight scenes and car chases. But anything that’s vaguely emotional in David Coggeshall’s script for Matchbox: The Movie falls flat, from the dad jokes to the corny homespun wisdom. Even seasoned ensemble cast members like Arturo Castro, John Cena, and Sam Richardson can’t breathe life into this programmatic, by-creative-committee dreck. It’s almost as if what made Barbie so special was its creators and not the meta-meaning that they projected onto their toy subjects.


Tell that to the poor kids and parents who will have to sit through a simultaneously maudlin and emotionally stillborn flashback/flash-forward preamble that struggles to connect the Matchbox toys that a group of middle school friends played with to the rote globetrotting spy shenanigans that they get up to as adults.


An early scene establishes, mostly through syrupy dialogue and a treacly score, that these kids used to love playing with Matchbox toys because it made them feel less alone. No actual footage of children playing with Matchbox toys is shown, of course. But we do hear about how small-town mechanic and surrogate dad Cal Smalley (dear lord, it’s Bill Camp slumming) treated the kids around him, including his gearhead niece Aimee (soon to be played by Jessica Biel) and future CIA covert operative Sean (eventually played by Cena).


The plot trails after Sean and his friends, now grown and newly reunited after Cal’s untimely death, as they’re reluctantly involved in a rogue CIA agent’s plot to steal and deploy a nuclear warhead. At first there’s some mystery as to who’s the traitor among Sean’s CIA pals, but it’s soon untangled by Sean and his friends, including the heavy-machinery-operating Crosby (Richardson) and his helicopter-piloting wife Charmaine (Teyonah Parris).


There’s some generic tension between Sean and his old pals, who spend most of the movie poking fun of Sean’s blandly cartoonish colleagues and lifestyle, as well as their own generic behavior once they’re slotted into Sean’s world, like when their motorcycle-riding schoolteacher buddy Ted (Castro) imitates Terminator 2: Judgment Day by shooting a truck with a shotgun, winking at us that, “Arnold made that look so much easier.” Soon after that, Ted kicks a guy out of a truck right after he throws a grenade at them; right before the guy blows up, Ted says: “Enjoy retirement.” It’s unclear what the joke here is, but presumably it’s on the viewers if we’re expecting much beyond DreamWorks-bland pop culture references and flop-sweat-soaked kitsch.


Among the movie’s stacked cast, nobody comes across like they know what they’re doing, except maybe Corey Stoll, who makes a meal of his one-note supporting role. Everyone else succumbs to their deliberately cheesy and often embarrassingly unfunny dialogue, the worst of which is meant to be somewhat dramatic, like when Sean’s stern CIA handler Ace (Danai Gurira) observes that, “Home doesn’t exist for people like us.”


The jokes aren’t much better though, like when Charmaine blows up bad guys with a missile and says, “Bye, bitch.” That over-the-top line and scenario might’ve been funny if the filmmakers showcased Parris’ comic line delivery instead of the bland computer-generated chaos. As it is, the scene’s a perfect example of the mirthless and tonally berserk Matchbox: The Movie.


It’s still disappointing to see scene-stealing performers like Cena and Richardson reduced to tedious jokes that only underscore how thin their characterizations are, and how rushed their performances seem. They don’t talk like human beings or even like knowing archetypes, but rather as machines tasked with delivering schematic laugh lines and unconvincing dramatic kickers. There’s no meaningful distinction between the unintentionally funny earnestness—”We’re here for you, Sean, ride or die”—and painfully unfunny punchlines, like when Richardson snarks “How original” when two characters appear to ride off into the sunset.


Matchbox: The Movie does fitfully come alive whenever it’s a John Cena showcase and not a tiresome group comedy. In these moments, Cena, Hargrave, and their stunt guys make Sean look like he could be an action hero worth caring about…until Cena must gracelessly muscle his way through some more rough dialogue, like when Sean snaps at his friends that his big “mistake wasn’t going away [from home], but coming back.”


The biggest problem with Matchbox: The Movie isn’t that it’s a dumb, by-the-numbers action movie, but rather that it doesn’t know how to be both a parody of that kind of movie and an emotionally resonant defense of camaraderie-instilling group play. Barbie, and to a lesser extent all three of Christopher Miller and Phil Lord’s Lego Movies, made that balancing act look easy. Hargrave’s clearance-section knock-off suggests otherwise.

items.title: As I Begin Replaying All Of Kingdom Hearts, What Do I Hope To Learn About A Series I Love?
items.author: Kenneth Shepard
items.summary: Hello and welcome to the first entry of Guiding Key, Kotaku’s new Kingdom Hearts book club where we’re going to go through every single game in Square Enix’s
items.text:
Hello and welcome to the first entry of Guiding Key, Kotaku’s new Kingdom Hearts book club where we’re going to go through every single game in Square Enix’s Disney/Final Fantasy crossover until we reach Kingdom Hearts IV’s launch in late 2027. Today is October 8, and that means Square just put out the Kingdom Hearts I~III Collection on PS5, Xbox Series X/S, and Switch 2, so if you’re looking to take part in our year-long retrospective, there’s a decent place to start. If you’re just following along and have already played these games, we’d definitely still love to hear from you as we go.

To start things off, before we actually get into the whole playing-the-game part in the next entry, I wanted to talk about my history with Kingdom Hearts and what I’m personally hoping to get out of this playthrough leading up to KHIV. Though it’s a bit unorthodox, Kingdom Hearts was actually my first Square game, one my brother and I rented for our PS2 back in the day. This was before we had a memory card, so we just played through the stuff on Destiny Islands and Traverse Town over and over. And even before I could play the rest of the game, I knew this was something that was going to change my brain chemistry.

Even though I was getting into anime such as Pokémon and Dragon Ball Z at the time, I hadn’t much been exposed to the kind of emotionally explosive storytelling Kingdom Hearts loves. The series wears its, er, heart, on its sleeve and at that young age, I hadn’t really encountered anything like it. The game acted as my gateway into Final Fantasy, and was one of my earliest examples of a reasonably complex action RPG. Perhaps the most precious memory I have of it, and of the series as a whole, is that the ending of this game was the first time a video game ever made me cry. I was in the fifth grade and only had so many words for the emotions I was feeling, and the second Utada Hikaru’s “Simple and Clean” kicked in in the final minutes, I was done. I was sobbing in my sister’s bedroom (where the PlayStation 2 was), and I had never done that before.

My relationship with the series was strong for a while. I adored Chain of Memories as a Riku diehard, I scoured the internet leading up to Kingdom Hearts II’s launch in some of my earliest experiences with social media, and Hikaru’s themes remained on repeat in minimized YouTube videos on my Internet browser.

In the years that followed, Kingdom Hearts continued to be a part of my life, but I was never quite in the thick of it as I was for those first three games. I still played them and kept up with the decade-and-change saga that was waiting for the next numbered game. It just wasn’t something I was as deeply invested in, and by the time Kingdom Hearts III came out, I was mostly there to find out if and how Square Enix could wrap up the games’ notoriously convoluted story of light, darkness, and the power of friendship. Like a lot of people, I wasn’t big on Kingdom Hearts III, but would have been pretty content to leave the series behind at that point. Square Enix and Disney were not about to let this train stop there, though, and thus we’re getting a whole new arc. After 25 years, Kingdom Hearts has woven an elaborate tale that is surprisingly complex for something Disney has not only greenlit, but seems to be doubling down on heading into Kingdom Hearts IV.

Outside of my writing here at Kotaku, I co-host a book club–style podcast called Normandy FM, and something I talk about there a lot is that, as time goes by, a lot of video games get distorted in the public eye as memes and in-jokes become the common way we discuss them. It’s disheartening to see something people put a lot of work into get boiled down to a caricature of itself, and that’s why I like doing that show: it gives us a chance to interrogate the way people’s tongue-in-cheek shorthand for a creative work somehow becomes all people really every say about it. To me, a lot of the arguments that Kingdom Hearts’ story is “too complicated” feel like that, typically pushed by people whose idea of actual criticism is to simply spout a bunch of out-of-context proper nouns and call it proof that an entire series of games is “too complicated,” because it has words and phrases you won’t understand unless you spend some time with the actual games.

To me, going back and playing through an entire series again is a chance to examine it for what it actually is, rather than what the passage of time and the claims of bad actors say it is. I want to dissect Kingdom Hearts for what Square Enix actually put into the world, and part of that involves talking about its very complex web of stories, but I also want to pinpoint exactly where that complication began. Though Square Enix has gone to great lengths to fill in gaps with complex lore that has expanded Kingdom Hearts’ story far beyond a Disney crossover, it was, at one time, much more straightforward than it eventually became. Something I’m particularly curious to see as we go through these games together is just when it starts to feel like that switch flips. Sora, Riku, and Kairi started out as a bunch of kids who wanted to see other worlds, only to find that their very existence on the beaches of Destiny Islands was far more significant than it seemed at the time. When did this shift start? Were the clues always there, or did Tetsuya Nomura decide at some point to start adding a lot more ingredients to the pie?

We’re all gonna find out this stuff together! I’ll be doing occasional blogs about each game (all will be categorized under the Guiding Key tag) as I go through, with big tentpole check-ins every month. The full Guiding Key schedule is as follows:

Kingdom Hearts: October-December 2026

Kingdom Hearts: Chain of Memories: January 2027

Kingdom Hearts II: February-April 2027

Kingdom Hearts 358/2 Days and Re:Coded: May 2027

Kingdom Hearts: Birth by Sleep: June 2027

Kingdom Hearts Dream Drop Distance and A Fragmentary Passage: July 2027

A watch through of the unplayable mobile games Kingdom Hearts Union χ Dark Road: August 2027

Kingdom Hearts III and the Re:Mind DLC: August-October 2027

Kingdom Hearts Melody of Memory: November 2027

Kingdom Hearts IV: Late 2027

items.title: Ambitious “Control Resonant” Challenges Expectations, Rewards Creativity
items.author: Brian Tallerico

items.text:
Even though people often love to point out this site’s namesake’s opinion on video games, since we began this coverage, we’ve tried to write about where the form intersects with film in cinematic franchises like “Silent Hill,” “Uncharted,” and “Resident Evil.” While playing the absolutely brilliant “Control Resonant,” I kept thinking of some of the most ambitious, game-changing science fiction films of all time, obvious influences like “The Matrix” and “Inception.”

But I also found myself pondering the work of David Lynch. How do “Twin Peaks” and Remedy Entertainment’s masterpiece intersect? It’s in a creator’s willingness to push boundaries, to use the visual language of dreams, and to find emotional grounding in the impossible. Creative Director Mikael Kasurinen has said via the review guide, “We wanted to make something that provokes. Something that feels like nothing you’ve played before.” Mission accomplished.

The excellent “Control” ended with hero Jesse Faden finding her brother Dylan, cleansing him of the infection by the all-powerful Hiss, and leaving him and the place known as The Oldest House under lockdown. Jesse became the Director of the FBC (Federal Bureau of Control) and promised to figure out a way to fix whatever had broken reality in New York City, allowing enemies from an extradimensional space to invade Gotham. Come to think of it: With its reality-shaking vision of Lovecraftian creatures that might literally be from Hell, “Control” has a bit of “Event Horizon” in its DNA, too.

Seven years after the Hiss invaded the Oldest House, Jesse wakes up Dylan and promptly disappears. Dylan becomes the hero of “Resonant,” which is one of many elements that give it a different aesthetic from its predecessor. One thing that takes a bit of getting used to is that this is not “Control 2” for a reason. It is a very different experience, trading the tight location work of the Oldest House for open-world gameplay with multiple zones and far more freedom of choice.

Early in “Resonant,” Dylan aligns with an FBC agent named Zoe de Vera, a companion who speaks to Dylan through the PS5 controller. You work with Zoe to figure out how an event called the “Patterning” has divided New York City from reality, leading to the invasion by thousands of creatures that want Dylan dead. As in many open-world games, you’re free to roam as Dylan, though the developers brilliantly layer in new powers for Faden that unlock new regions, combat approaches, and different enemies. The game balances wiping out packs of routine enemies, the occasional fight with a Resonant or boss, and alternating story and main missions.

The “Resonant” developers lean into significantly more RPG elements with Dylan than they did with Jesse. Skill trees, magical items, various weapons to choose for a loadout—it’s all deeply customizable. That said, combat works similarly no matter the angle you take. It’s mostly melee-based combat with a steady flow of strike-and-dodge mechanics, but you can also unlock special powers through game progress, including summoning allies to fight alongside you and hurling projectiles.

My first few hours with “Resonant” were mixed. It truly does require you to recalibrate expectations after the relatively linear first game. I found myself wandering New York City, unsure what to do and wondering why the story missions were kicking my ass. The answer is that this game doesn’t just encourage exploration; it requires it. You can’t push through only the story missions in “Resonant” because you won’t be strong enough. You need to complete side missions to level up and become strong enough to take on enemies like Resonants, but you also need to explore the city, wandering into places like laundromats and gyms to find upgrade resources.

After a couple of hours, “Resonant” kicks into gear and doesn’t look back. Several missions in this game rank among the best of the last several years, including one where you escape a sinkhole and one where Dylan plays with shadows of himself and a younger Jesse that are unquestionably moving. This game does things narratively that would terrify most writers’ rooms in games, TV, or film. The missions can be so wildly unpredictable—one minute you’re guiding a magical cat to fight a demon and the next you’re battling mold spore creatures that look like the kin of Bloaters from “The Last of Us.”

You can never quite tell where “Resonant” is going, which gives it the storytelling power of great film or television. It’s got enough authorial decisions through customization and exploration to make you feel like you’re in “Control,” but it also contains remarkably confident writing, not just in plot but dialogue and character work as well.

And then there’s the navigation. After a few clunky hours where even getting around NYC can feel tough, Dylan gains two powers: one that can pull him to points on buildings above him, and one that can basically turn the entire world on its axis. You know that scene in “Inception” wherein Elliot Page’s character flips the city on itself and they “walk up” a street?

Now imagine that in gameplay. While it sounds almost impossibly disorienting, the developers use it in just the right places, allowing Dylan to control not just through superpowered combat but by shifting the entire world around him. It leads to some of the most stunning level design in years, especially late in the game when the entire setting becomes pliable.

What Remedy Entertainment is doing with the “Alan Wake” and “Control” games is unlike anything else on the market. They’re accomplishing what so many great artists have done: Pushing back against the rules and expectations put on their form by so many years of conforming creators. We can argue all day about the definitions of art, but the ambition in “Control Resonant” is a sibling of what we so often look for in literature, film, or theatre, too. It’s that charge we all get when we can tell something is working in a way we haven’t really experienced before. Maybe more than any game this year, “Resonant” has it.

The Publisher provided a review copy of this title. It is now available on PS5, Xbox Series, and Windows.

blocks.x: Even though people often love to point out this site’s namesake’s opinion on video games, since we began this coverage, we’ve tried to write about where the form intersects with film in cinematic franchises like “Silent Hill,” “Uncharted,” and “Resident Evil.” While playing the absolutely brilliant “Control Resonant,” I kept thinking of some of the most ambitious, game-changing science fiction films of all time, obvious influences like “The Matrix” and “Inception.”

But I also found myself pondering the work of David Lynch. How do “Twin Peaks” and Remedy Entertainment’s masterpiece intersect? It’s in a creator’s willingness to push boundaries, to use the visual language of dreams, and to find emotional grounding in the impossible. Creative Director Mikael Kasurinen has said via the review guide, “We wanted to make something that provokes. Something that feels like nothing you’ve played before.” Mission accomplished.

The excellent “Control” ended with hero Jesse Faden finding her brother Dylan, cleansing him of the infection by the all-powerful Hiss, and leaving him and the place known as The Oldest House under lockdown. Jesse became the Director of the FBC (Federal Bureau of Control) and promised to figure out a way to fix whatever had broken reality in New York City, allowing enemies from an extradimensional space to invade Gotham. Come to think of it: With its reality-shaking vision of Lovecraftian creatures that might literally be from Hell, “Control” has a bit of “Event Horizon” in its DNA, too.

Seven years after the Hiss invaded the Oldest House, Jesse wakes up Dylan and promptly disappears. Dylan becomes the hero of “Resonant,” which is one of many elements that give it a different aesthetic from its predecessor. One thing that takes a bit of getting used to is that this is not “Control 2” for a reason. It is a very different experience, trading the tight location work of the Oldest House for open-world gameplay with multiple zones and far more freedom of choice.

Early in “Resonant,” Dylan aligns with an FBC agent named Zoe de Vera, a companion who speaks to Dylan through the PS5 controller. You work with Zoe to figure out how an event called the “Patterning” has divided New York City from reality, leading to the invasion by thousands of creatures that want Dylan dead. As in many open-world games, you’re free to roam as Dylan, though the developers brilliantly layer in new powers for Faden that unlock new regions, combat approaches, and different enemies. The game balances wiping out packs of routine enemies, the occasional fight with a Resonant or boss, and alternating story and main missions.

The “Resonant” developers lean into significantly more RPG elements with Dylan than they did with Jesse. Skill trees, magical items, various weapons to choose for a loadout—it’s all deeply customizable. That said, combat works similarly no matter the angle you take. It’s mostly melee-based combat with a steady flow of strike-and-dodge mechanics, but you can also unlock special powers through game progress, including summoning allies to fight alongside you and hurling projectiles.

My first few hours with “Resonant” were mixed. It truly does require you to recalibrate expectations after the relatively linear first game. I found myself wandering New York City, unsure what to do and wondering why the story missions were kicking my ass. The answer is that this game doesn’t just encourage exploration; it requires it. You can’t push through only the story missions in “Resonant” because you won’t be strong enough. You need to complete side missions to level up and become strong enough to take on enemies like Resonants, but you also need to explore the city, wandering into places like laundromats and gyms to find upgrade resources.

After a couple of hours, “Resonant” kicks into gear and doesn’t look back. Several missions in this game rank among the best of the last several years, including one where you escape a sinkhole and one where Dylan plays with shadows of himself and a younger Jesse that are unquestionably moving. This game does things narratively that would terrify most writers’ rooms in games, TV, or film. The missions can be so wildly unpredictable—one minute you’re guiding a magical cat to fight a demon and the next you’re battling mold spore creatures that look like the kin of Bloaters from “The Last of Us.”

You can never quite tell where “Resonant” is going, which gives it the storytelling power of great film or television. It’s got enough authorial decisions through customization and exploration to make you feel like you’re in “Control,” but it also contains remarkably confident writing, not just in plot but dialogue and character work as well.

And then there’s the navigation. After a few clunky hours where even getting around NYC can feel tough, Dylan gains two powers: one that can pull him to points on buildings above him, and one that can basically turn the entire world on its axis. You know that scene in “Inception” wherein Elliot Page’s character flips the city on itself and they “walk up” a street?

Now imagine that in gameplay. While it sounds almost impossibly disorienting, the developers use it in just the right places, allowing Dylan to control not just through superpowered combat but by shifting the entire world around him. It leads to some of the most stunning level design in years, especially late in the game when the entire setting becomes pliable.

What Remedy Entertainment is doing with the “Alan Wake” and “Control” games is unlike anything else on the market. They’re accomplishing what so many great artists have done: Pushing back against the rules and expectations put on their form by so many years of conforming creators. We can argue all day about the definitions of art, but the ambition in “Control Resonant” is a sibling of what we so often look for in literature, film, or theatre, too. It’s that charge we all get when we can tell something is working in a way we haven’t really experienced before. Maybe more than any game this year, “Resonant” has it.

items.text:
While Japanese has tons of English loanwords, English actually borrows quite a bit from Japanese as well. Words like sushi, karate, or tsunami are so commonly used that it might be easy to forget that they’re loanwords from Japan.

Let’s discover some common Japanese loanwords in English, covering some of the old and some of the new, but this blog is by no means exhaustive. By the end of this article, who knows? New words are probably being borrowed at this very moment.

Why Do Japanese and English Borrow so Many Words From Each Other?

Since Japanese and English come from very different places with distinct cultures, cuisines, and geographic characteristics or phenomena, the more exposed we are to each other’s cultures, the more new concepts and words we encounter. It makes sense that English would just adopt the words for Japanese food items like “sushi” or “ramen.”

However, the word tsunami is also of Japanese origin. It just so happens that English had no word for huge tidal waves, so it borrowed tsunami from Japanese. Often when a word sufficiently describes something we don’t have a word for, we just adopt it into our language. As you are probably well aware, Japanese quite often does the same.

You’ve probably experienced what could be called the katakana glitch. You see a katakana word, and you just can’t figure out what it is until you mouth it, then you finally figure out that biiru (ビール) is actually “beer”. You probably can think of many more English loanwords in Japanese, such as soccer, or sakkaa (サッカー), and even modern slang like rizz, or rizu (リズ). New words are crossing over, perhaps because the internet and pop culture spread new trends faster than ever before.

Note that this doesn’t always happen; when baseball was introduced to Japan, they made their own word for the sport, yakyuu (野球), which is made up of the words field, or 野 (ya), and ball, 球 (kyuu).

Japanese Loanwords Used in English for Food and Entertainment

In 2013, UNESCO named Japanese food an intangible cultural heritage. The flavors and practices associated with Japanese food are unique. Many of the Japanese loanwords in English reflect that uniqueness. Similarly, many aspects of Japanese entertainment tend to originate in Japan, and the English words borrowed from Japanese show that.

A lot of these loanwords are originally written in kanji, hiragana, or katakana. If you need to review hiragana and katakana, head to this article.

1. Karaoke (カラオケ)

Did you even know this was a Japanese word before Karaoke actually came into contact with Japan or the language? It has roots in the words: kara (空), meaning “empty,” and oke (オケ), meaning “orchestra.” So, together the word actually means orchestraAlso, have you seen anyone do karaoke like the Japanese?

2. Sudoku (すどく)

If you’ve played sudoku and understand it, more power to you. This game and its title originated in Japan in 1984 and have since become very popular worldwide. The su comes from suji or suu (数), meaning number, and the doku (独) means single. The overall aim of the game is to get numbers to appear once in squares in a grid. So literally, the numbers must remain single. Or suuji wa dokushin ni kagiru (数字は独身に限る), which was the original title of the game.

Europeans actually played a similar game in the 18th century. In the 1980s, a Japanese publisher distributed sudoku, which turned into a huge hit and has been popular ever since.

3. Pachinko　(パチンコ)

Hard to spend any time in Japan and not see a pachinko parlor. Pachinko is a kind of pinball game played in arcade games or, more commonly, gambling parlors. Japanese people like to make words that mimic or represent the sound you hear, like the bees buzzing or the snake hissing. The word pachinko is partly made up of a Japanese onomatopoeia. The first part, pachin, is from the sound that the metal pinball makes as it hits an obstacle. The ko is a diminutive suffix that means something like ‘little’.

4. Soy (sauce, beans)

Tofu and miso are obviously Japanese loanwords, but soy? Yes, apparently it comes from しょうゆ (shoyu), which is Japanese for soy sauce. The actual Japanese term for the bean is daizu. Edamame, which are green soybeans, is also commonly used in English.

5. Tamari (たまりしょうゆ)

This one is kind of hip these days. Many recipe bloggers suggest using tamari as a ‘healthy’ alternative to regular soy sauce. Tamari is richer, thicker, and less salty than regular soy sauce, but it is also made from fermented soybeans.

6. Shiitake, maitake, matsutake, and enoki mushrooms (椎茸、舞茸、松茸、えのき)

Did I miss any? Many Japanese mushroom names have been carried over and used as-is in English. The most popular of these might be shiitake, which is often pronounced without the second ‘i’, resulting in shitake.

7. Umami (旨味)

Umami is probably one of the most popular Japanese loanwords in English, being used all the time to describe a distinct savory flavor. This term is a relatively recent adoption into the English language, and it’s somewhat new to Japanese as well.

The word was first coined in 1908 when a Japanese scientist used the word to describe the “5th taste,” which is savoriness. In both Japanese and English, umami generally describes the savory flavor you would find in cooked meats, soy sauce, and mushrooms.

8. Dashi　(だし)

No mention of washoku can exclude dashi, stock made from fish or kelp that is used as the base for many Japanese dishes. Dashi is commonly used in English to mean the same thing.

9. Katsu (curry or chicken katsu)　(かつ)

Katsu refers to cutlets of meat that are breaded using panko and deep-fried. The cutlets are usually pork or chicken. Katsu is served with a sauce or with curry. In fact, in some places overseas, katsu curry has become so popular that the term is used to mean all Japanese curry.

10. Panko　(パン粉)

You might have guessed this from the previous entry, but panko is breadcrumbs. They are commonly used in Japanese cooking and the product and the name have crossed over into English-speaking cultures.

The word panko is actually a combination of a loanword that didn’t come from English and the original Japanese word. “Pan” came from the Portuguese language, pao, and ko (粉) is a Japanese word that means “flour” or “dust”.

The biggest difference between panko and standard breadcrumbs is that panko is made from bread without crusts. Panko’s crustless white bread is coarsely ground into airy, large flakes that give fried foods a light, crunchy coating.

11. Amazake (甘酒)

Making the list of words of Japanese origin recently recorded in the Oxford English Dictionary, amazake is a sweet, fermented drink made from rice. Unlike sake, which is also made from rice, amazake is not alcoholic. It literally means sweet (ama) sake.

12. Manga (漫画)

These loanwords are used the same way in English as they are in Japanese. One distinction is that while manga means comics in general in Japan, the term typically means Japanese comics in English.

13. Anime (アニメ)

Probably the most popular loanword used all the time in English is アニメ (anime), which ironically comes from the word “animation” borrowed from English. But in English, “anime” specifically refers to Japanese animation even though in Japanese it refers to all animation. This term is a great example of words being traded back and forth between two languages.

14. Emoji　(絵文字)

Texting and instant messaging is just not the same without emoji, graphics that help express an emotion when words are just not enough. But the cute, yellow pictogram you’ve been using on your iPhone? The word came from the Japanese language. The kanji 絵 (え) means “picture” and 文字 (もじ) means “character” or “letter.” You might learn some new emoji from the Emojipedia online.

Japanese Loanwords Used in English for Sport and Martial Arts

Japanese martial arts are known the world over by their Japanese names. These are quite established loanwords, and the sports themselves continue to gain devotees.

15. Judo　(柔道)

Japanese martial arts are well-known throughout the English-speaking world, by their Japanese names. Judo, a defensive martial art, is no exception. The term originates from soft, gentle (柔; juu) and way, road (道; do). Judo is an Olympic event, and practitioners are usually called judoka (柔道家).

When you’re saying the word “judo” in Japanese, remember to elongate the first syllable: Ju-u-dou. In English, however, you can shorten it.

16. Jujutsu　(柔術)

Precursor to judo, this is also a Japanese unarmed martial art. The first part of the term, juu means gentle, just like in judo and the jutsu (術) means skill or art. There are variant spellings in English, including jiu-jitsu or ju-jitsu. It is also the origin of the name of the famous martial art, Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu.

However, historical evidence shows that Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu (BJJ) comes from Judo, but at the time Judo was still being called “Ju-Jutsu,” which is why BJJ has its name today rather than “Brazilian Judo.”

17. Karate　(空手)

Karate is definitely one of those Japanese loanwords that almost feels like it’s always been in English. The term originates from empty (kara) and hand (te), meaning fighting with bare hands. But the history actually gets more interesting.

Karate originates with the indigenous people of Okinawa, who referred to their martial arts as 手(te or tii in Okinawan). But because the Okinawans traded so much with China, Chinese martial arts heavily influenced Karate, so it was initially called “Chinese hand” (唐手), pronounced the same as we know it today. Eventually, after Japan took over Okinawa, the name was changed to 空手 (karate).

18. Kendo　(剣道)

Another Japanese martial art that was simply imported into English, it consists of participants using bamboo swords and wearing protective gear based loosely on samurai armor. Ken means “sword” and do means “way.”

19. Sumo　(相撲)

Often suffixed with ‘wrestling’ in English, sumo means to fight. It’s not just the word that has crossed borders. Many non-Japanese people have succeeded as sumo wrestlers, in what is perceived to be a closed and very traditional world. Check out this quick guide to sumo related terms to learn a bit more about the sport.

Japanese Loanwords Used in English for Performing and Literary Arts

From the theater to the page, traditional Japanese performing and literary arts have become well-known in English-speaking cultures.

20. Kabuki　(歌舞伎)

This is a kind of Japanese theater. The Online Etymology Dictionary cites two possible origins of this Japanese loanword. One is that kabuki comes from the verb kabuku, meaning to deviate. The first kabuki performance was given in a shrine by a girl, dressed as a man, which was outside of the norm. The other explanation is that kabuki means ‘art of song and dance,’ from ka (song), bu (dance), and ki (art, skill).

21. Noh　(能)

In Noh theater, performers sing and dance while wearing masks. This loanword comes from the Japanese meaning ‘talent’.

22. Tanka　(短歌)

A poem written using just five lines, tanka means short (tan) song (ka). In English, the poems typically use five lines and 31 syllables, but in Japanese, they are typically written in three lines.

23. Haiku (俳句)

If you’ve heard about haiku, you probably have the impression that it takes immense skill to craft them. These poems are written using a set number of syllables. The haiku consists of three lines, with five syllables in the first line, seven in the second, and five in the third.

Though haiku were originally written in Japanese, English poems following this pattern also go by the same name. Literally meaning light (haikai no) verse (ku), these poems are often about nature.

23. Senryu (川柳)

Senryu is a loanword that refers to another type of Japanese poetry that’s similar to haiku. It tends to talk about people, rather than nature. This form was named after a poet who frequently practiced it.

Other Japanese Loanwords We Use in English

From business to bedding and natural disasters, Japanese loanwords are used in many areas of life. The following words don’t fall neatly into the categories we have here. But they are still commonly used.

25. Tycoon (大君)

You’ve probably heard this word used a lot with another t-word, tech, as in tech tycoon. Its origins have little do with technology, however. Taikun was the name foreigners gave to the shogun (another loanword) when they came to Japan in the 1800s. Over time, taikun (great lord) became tycoon. Today, the word refers to someone of tremendous wealth and power.

26. Honcho　(班長)

This is another loanword often used alliteratively with head, as in head honcho, meaning leader. The term originates from Japanese han (group) and cho (leader), and was apparently picked up by foreigners in Japan during the second world war.

27. Skosh (少し: Sukoshi)

Have you ever noticed someone saying, “Just a skosh.” Maybe you’re asking if you need to add more salt when you are making soup. This loanword is a shortening of the Japanese sukoshi, meaning a little. It was adopted by the US servicemen when they were stationed in Japan after World War II. It is used in the same way in English and carries the nuance of a really tiny amount.

28. Zen　(善)

This loanword originates from the Japanese school of Zen Buddhism that focuses on meditation. In common use in English, zen means calm and peaceful, and doesn’t explicitly refer to Buddhism.

29. Futon　(布団)

Futon is one of those loanwords that perhaps many people have forgotten is, in fact, a loanword. It’s used to describe a flat mattress that can be rolled up, which is traditional bedding in Japan. However, in English, people refer to couches that have pull-out beds as futons. The fu in this loanword means sheet or cloth, and the ton means group.

30. Ikigai (生きがい)

Ikigai, as a concept, has been making waves in the English-speaking world in recent years. Iki means life and gai means value, so the term translates to ‘reason for being’. The idea is that with a reason for being or a purpose, people can live more fulfilling lives, as those lives get longer.

31. Tsunami (津波)

Originating from harbor (tsu) and wave (nami), this word has been in use in many unfortunate circumstances recently. As with the original Japanese, it describes a large sea wave caused by an earthquake. Tsunami has also been used in a figurative sense to mean a large and sudden amount of something.

32. Samurai (侍)

Many words from Japanese history are usually adopted directly into English, and samurai is no exception. Samurai describes a specific warrior class that only existed in the context of Japan. Calling them “Japanese knights” just wouldn’t capture what they were and the place they had in Japanese society.

Likewise, many other historical Japanese terms for different social positions or figures, like shogun, daimyo, or even ninja, are simply borrowed in English.

33. Katana (刀)

While katana actually just means “sword,” in English it has come to refer to the specific Japanese sword with its characteristic curved blade that was used by the samurai. Likely due to its unique aesthetics, carefully crafted by skilled blacksmiths, it caught the attention of foreigners. Thus, now we use the word katana to describe the iconic sword from Japan.

34. Kimono (着物)

The kimono is a beautiful, elegant garment that has come to be known as the national dress of Japan. So, there’s no question why English adopted the word kimono to describe this iconic piece of clothing. There isn’t even an equivalent type of clothing to the kimono in English-speaking countries; while there are dresses and robes, none of them are quite a kimono.

35. Shinkansen (新幹線)

While English has the word “bullet train,” it’s not uncommon for people to opt to use the word “shinkansen” instead. Japan’s efficient transportation system, particularly the bullet train, has become such an image of the nation that shinkansen is now widely known in English. Often when people visit Japan, they might say they want to ride the “shinkansen” rather than the “bullet train.”

Conclusion:

You might be surprised how many words the English language adopts from Japanese alone. You’ve no doubt been using many of them and as the English language continues to borrow words from Japanese, you’ll end up using even more Japanese, in English. The truth is, languages constantly borrow from each other, showing how we exchange ideas all the time.

As a matter of fact, Japanese doesn’t just borrow words from English. To find out more, read our blog: Loan Words in Japanese that Don’t Come from English!

If you can’t make it to Japan yet, an online course is one of the best ways to start your Japanese language journey.
